narration.full_text:
Hello students! In this section, we'll dive into the fascinating world of control and coordination in living organisms. We'll explore how different activities are regulated and integrated to ensure survival and proper responses to the environment. Control and coordination is the process by which different activities of an organism are regulated and integrated so that it can respond properly to internal and external stimuli. Living organisms perform many activities at the same time. These activities must be controlled and coordinated to maintain balance and survival. All living organisms respond and react to changes in the environment around them. These changes are called stimuli. Stimuli can be anything from light, heat, cold, smell, or touch. Both plants and animals respond to stimuli, but they do so in different ways. In animals, control and coordination are primarily managed by two main systems: the Nervous system and the Endocrine system. Today, we will focus on the Nervous System.

In biological systems, control and coordination are essential functions, primarily handled by nervous and muscular tissues. The nervous tissue is a highly organized network of nerve cells, also known as neurons. These specialized cells are responsible for conducting information throughout the body in the form of electrical impulses, facilitating communication between different parts. The nervous system itself is a comprehensive network of conducting tissues that receives stimuli and transmits this information to various parts of the body, forming an intricate web of nerves. The fundamental units that constitute this complex nervous system are called nerve cells or neurons. These neurons are crucial for transmitting information. For instance, receptors, which detect stimuli, pass this information to the brain through a specific type of nerve cell called sensory neurons. Once the brain processes this information, another type of neuron, known as motor neurons, transmits the response from the brain to the effector organs. These effector organs are primarily muscles and glands, which then carry out the appropriate action or response. The information that travels through neurons is referred to as a nerve impulse. This impulse is a combination of chemical and electrical signals. These impulses are typically carried towards the cell body of a neuron by structures called dendrites, which act like antennae, receiving signals from other neurons.
